There are only a few absolutes in life; everything else is subject to context.

If someone holds a gun to a stranger's head, they are in a position of great power; the opposite is true if the person the gun is being pointed at happens to be holding a dead-mans switch that will detonate a bomb in the center of a major city. The relative power shifts again if the person holding the gun doesn't care about the people in the city and simply wants the one with the dead-man's switch to hand over his wallet. The power shifts yet again if the person holding the dead-man's switch is a drug addict, doesn't care if he lives or dies, and cares only for the LSD he's got hidden in his wallet.

The point here is that context is important, and power lies in the ability to change it. In the story above, there are two major characters: the one with the gun(GUN) and the other with the dead-man's switch (DMS). But suppose a third character was added. We'll call him the ruthless landlord (RLL) that GUN owes money to. The only reason that GUN want's DMS's wallet is to find money to pay RLL so that he doesn't get evicted; if only RLL would give GUN a break on his rent, there would be no need to kill DMS and consequently everyone in the major city. Suddenly RLL, who beforehand was unmentioned has become a major character, and has a tremendous amount of power over the people in the city. If DMS's drug dealer lives in the city, then the latter has a great deal of interest in keeping DMS alive, and thus RLL now has power over the dealer and, by extension, DMS. Context Matters.

But who gets to decide who is a major character? Who gets to tell the story? This is a deeper level of power. Up to this point, I've been telling the story. But suppose that its the mayor of the city that's telling the story, and suppose further that DMS is his beloved son that he would do anything for. Suddenly, the story might go something like, "There's a man holding my son at gunpoint, threatening to kill everyone in the city". Technically true, but leaving out so many details that reality becomes warped. Yet perhaps this is all the mayor can see from behind is rose-tinted glasses while viewing his son. Context matters.

But there is still a deeper level. Controlling the story is powerful, but who controls the language with which we tell it? Words and their connotations circumscribe the boundaries of communication, and our experiences shape what amount to our prototypical understanding of a concept. Returning to the story, suppose this entire time by "gun" I meant a water pistol. Suppose further that when I said "bomb", I was talking about this. Suddenly everything changes because the prototypical understanding of the story teller was fundamentally different from that of the listeners. Context matters.
